Clusters and Mapping

GIS & clustering

For spatial analysis, several base layers and functions are provided for mapping and clustering detection. The R package “sf” is used in most spatial transformations and analysis. Geo coded data can be mapped both statically and interactively.

The named list variable geo_sets stores paths to often used base layers. For example geo_sets$isd returns the path to a layer of independent school districts. The next table shows the name and the layer available, all of which are polygons stored as “sf” objects and have a coordinate reference system set epsg:4326

Name Layer
ZCTA Tarrant Zip Code Tabulation Areas
tarrant_border Tarrant County boundaries as a polygon
tarrant_tracts Census tracts in Tarrant County
tarrant_blocks Census blocks in Tarrant County
tarrant_cities Boundaries of partially or wholly contained cities
surrounding_borders Borders of counties surrounding Tarrant
isd Independent School Districts

Each of the layers can be loaded using load_tarrant_spatial() or readRDS(). The load_tarrant_spatial(.name, .crs) takes one of the names in the table above and by default returns the layer with a Coordinate Reference System (CRS) of ‘4326’. The crs can be used to have the spatial layer in a different coordinate reference system. You can also use the base R function readRDS() and give it the path to the layer using the geo_sets list varibale. Here is how each method can be used to load a layer.

library(tarr,  quietly = TRUE)
#> ── Attaching tarr ecosystem ──
#> ✔ rage
#> ✔ tarr.pop
library(sf,    quietly = TRUE)
#> Linking to GEOS 3.13.1, GDAL 3.11.0, PROJ 9.6.0; sf_use_s2() is TRUE

# load and add city boundaries using readRDS and geo_sets
other_counties <- readRDS(file = geo_sets$surrounding_borders)
plot(x = st_geometry(other_counties), border = "grey60")

# load the Tarrant County border then add it to the map
tarr_border <- load_tarrant_spatial("tarrant_border")
plot(x = st_geometry(tarr_border), border = "red", add = TRUE )


rm(cities, other_counties, tarr_border)
#> Warning in rm(cities, other_counties, tarr_border): object 'cities' not found

Mapping cases

Line lists of cases with latititude and longitude data can be mapped. Importantly, case lists from EpiTtax can include the lat/lon the residence of each case. For example, usng the package provided synthtic_outbreak data frame, make it a simple fetures (sf) POINTS object that can be mapped using the st_as_sf() function.

Several base map tiles from Google maps and Stadiamaps are also available in the package. These can be used for background to give points context in a non-interactive map. The tiles are stored in a list called base_map[.]


# get theTarrant County outline
county  <- load_tarrant_spatial("tarrant_border")

# Select the fooflu cases and make it an sf POINTS object
foo <- synthetic_outbreak[synthetic_outbreak$condition == "fooflu",] |> 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat")) 
  
# foo needs a crs, assign it from the county sf object
st_crs(foo) = st_crs(county)
  
# plot the "cases"  and county outline
plot(st_geometry(foo), col = "red3")
plot(st_geometry(county), add = TRUE, border = "navyblue", col = NA)

A static map

Density based algorithms are provided for identifying possiblespatial clusters.

foo_scan <- scan_cluster(points = foo, method = "HDBSCAN", eps = 5280*1.25, minPts = 7)
foo_scan

# Optional basemap layers

spat <- load_tarrant_spatial()

# Ensure geometry 
# cases_sf <- sf::st_as_sf(nbs, coords = c(lon,lat), crs = 4326)

# Cluster (example: HDBSCAN)
cl <- scan_cluster(
  x = cases_sf,
  method = hdbscan,
  minPts = 5
)

# Visualize (ggplot)
autoplot(cl) + map_theme

# Or with tmap
plot(cl)

# Inspect clustering internals
scan_object(cl)
get_unit(cl)

Tips - Prefer a projected CRS for distance-based clustering (choose one appropriate for your county/state). - HDBSCAN handles variable density better; DBSCAN is fast for well-separated clusters.
